title: What should we make of the violence in the Old Testament?
realQuestion:
In Deuteronomy and Joshua, God is described as commanding Israel to leave nothing alive in the cities of Canaan. In 1 Samuel, Saul loses his kingdom for sparing the Amalekite king and the livestock. These are not obscure passages.

The argument is about what a reader should conclude from them, and it is tagged interpretive because both sides can grant every fact — what the words say, when they were written, what happened in the ground — and still disagree about what those facts are evidence of.

The Christian answer is not one answer. Four incompatible readings are set out below, held by people who all take the text as authoritative, and each is objected to by other Christians as sharply as by anyone outside. Most people raised in a church have met one of them.

distinctions.label: Did the conquest happen as described?
distinctions.gloss: Largely no, and this is not contested by archaeologists of any persuasion: no mass invasion from outside, no matching destruction layers, Jericho's walls in ruins for a century before any plausible date. It matters less than it looks, because the moral objection is to a text presenting God as commanding it, and that stands whether or not it was carried out. Set out in the note below.

distinctions.label: Do these passages give good reason to reject the God the Bible describes?
distinctions.gloss: This is the argument on this page. Both sides agree about what the text says; they disagree about what kind of writing it is and what follows from it.

distinctions.label: Has religion caused more violence than it prevented?
distinctions.gloss: A different question, largely empirical, about institutions and history rather than about a text. Topic 18.

distinctions.label: Is the Bible reliable?
distinctions.gloss: The general question about the text's accuracy and authority. Several readings below turn on it — two of them abandon inerrancy openly — but the moral argument here runs whatever the answer. Topic 14.

glossary.definition: The Hebrew term in these passages, usually rendered 'devote to destruction' or 'utterly destroy'. Its range and force is one of the things scholars disagree about.

The idea, older than the modern debate, that God works within the limits of the culture he is speaking to rather than correcting everything at once. Calvin used it; the reading below applies it further than Calvin did.

The doctrine that Scripture contains no errors of any kind. Two of the readings below are available only to Christians who do not hold it, which is why the objection lands differently in different churches.

sides.label: The commands are not what a modern reader takes them to be

arguments.claim: 'Leave nothing alive' was standard exaggeration in ancient war writing, and the same books show survivors
arguments.explanation:
The best-known scholarly defence is about genre, and it is a claim about evidence rather than a plea. Egyptian, Moabite and Assyrian conquest accounts routinely say a people was annihilated and left without seed, in cases where we know from other records that the people continued.

The biblical text does the same thing to itself. Joshua reports total destruction; Judges, which continues the story, has Canaanites living everywhere. Paul Copan's argument is that a reader who takes '[[herem]] everything that breathes' as a body count is reading a battle report in a genre that did not exist yet, and that the internal contradiction is a signal about what kind of writing it is.

quote.text: Joshua's conventional warfare rhetoric was common in many other ancient Near Eastern military accounts in the second and first millennia B.C.
quote.author: Paul Copan
quote.work: Is God a Moral Monster? Making Sense of the Old Testament God

variants.label: The Israelites got God wrong, and the text records that
variants.heldBy: Peter Enns, Kenton Sparks; much of mainline and progressive scholarship
variants.oneLine: An ancient tribal people understood their God the way ancient tribal peoples did, and Scripture records that honestly rather than correcting it.
variants.summary:
On this reading the Bible is not a set of dictated propositions but the record of a people's developing understanding of God, including the parts they got wrong. Israel's neighbours all had war gods who granted victory and demanded the spoils; Israel wrote in that idiom because Israel lived in that world.

The theological claim is [[accommodation]]: God meets people where they are rather than starting with a lecture. What the text gives you is a true account of how Israel saw God at that stage, not a true account of God.

quote.text: God never told the Israelites to kill the Canaanites. The Israelites believed that God told them to kill the Canaanites.
quote.author: Peter Enns

variants.changesTheObjection: The genre objection cannot land, because this reading never claimed the commands were hyperbole. It agrees they read as real commands and says the report of them is mistaken — so an argument that the text has been strained to avoid its plain sense is answered by conceding the plain sense entirely.

objection.text: If the text can be wrong about this, what settles which parts are wrong? The reading needs a criterion, and the one usually offered — read the Old Testament through Jesus — is the very thing at issue, since the God of the conquest and the God of the Gospels are supposed to be the same. Without a criterion the method licenses removing whatever a given century finds uncomfortable, and the charge that the readings arrive in the order the moral pressure is applied is aimed squarely here.
objection.response: The criterion is stated and is not new: the tradition has read the Old Testament through Christ since the second century, and doing so openly is more honest than doing it while claiming to read flatly.

variants.label: The violent portraits are real, and must be read through the cross
variants.heldBy: Gregory Boyd; a strand of Anabaptist and nonviolent theology
variants.oneLine: God's character is fully revealed in a crucified man; where the Old Testament shows something else, it is showing God stooping to bear his people's misunderstanding.
variants.summary:
This reading refuses both of the usual exits. It does not soften the texts — Boyd insists they are as violent as they look — and it does not simply call them mistaken.

On the cross, God takes on an appearance that misrepresents him: a criminal, cursed, defeated. Boyd argues the violent portraits work the same way. God allowed himself to be depicted as his people could then conceive him, bearing the distortion rather than abandoning them, and the cross is what tells us it is a distortion.

quote.text: The Old Testament's violent portraits of God are not softened or set aside but read as God stooping to bear the distorted way his people conceived him, in the same self-emptying that reaches its full expression at the cross, where God again takes on an appearance that misrepresents his true character.
quote.author: Gregory A. Boyd
quote.work: The Crucifixion of the Warrior God
quote.locator: our summary of the cruciform thesis; not Boyd's wording

variants.changesTheObjection: The genre objection has nothing to work on. Boyd agrees the commands read as commands and that no philological result will soften them; he keeps the texts at full strength and relocates the question to what a revelation of that kind is doing. An argument that the hyperbole reading strains the Hebrew is not an argument against a reading that never invoked it.

objection.text: The method has no stopping rule. If a passage that misrepresents God is thereby revealing him by bearing the misrepresentation, then nothing in the text could ever count against the thesis, and conservative reviewers object that a reader may mark any passage as distortion. From the other direction the complaint is the opposite: the reading concedes the entire moral objection — these portraits are false, and terrible — and then declines to draw the conclusion.
objection.response: The stopping rule is the cross, which is a fixed point rather than a preference, and both objections are the intended cost: the method exists to keep the texts and the moral judgement at once.

counter.objection: Thom Stark's book-length response argues that the hyperbole reading does not survive the texts it is applied to. Conventional exaggeration about how thoroughly a city fell is one thing; a specific instruction to kill women, children and infants is another, and 1 Samuel 15 gives the list in detail. The reading also cuts the wrong way: if the language is conventional, then Israel's God is being made to speak in the idiom of the surrounding war gods, which is closer to the critic's account than to the defender's. Eric Seibert, writing as a Christian, presses the same point about what the defence costs.
counter.sharedPremise: it argues from the text itself and from what a high view of Scripture commits its holder to — that the words mean what a competent ancient reader would have taken them to mean, and that the specific and detailed commands cannot be dissolved by a convention that fits the general ones.
counter.response: The lists are themselves part of the formula, appearing in the same stereotyped order in non-biblical texts, and the comparative case for the convention is accepted well outside apologetics.

arguments.claim: It was judgement, and the objection assumes God is bound by the duties we owe each other
arguments.explanation:
This reading takes the text at face value and disputes the standard applied to it. The Canaanite cultures are described in Leviticus as practising child sacrifice; Genesis has God telling Abraham that his descendants will not return for four generations because the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete. The conquest is presented as a judgement long delayed.

The second half is a claim about relations. You may not take a life; a doctor may cut you open; a state may imprison you. What is permitted turns on the relation, and on William Lane Craig's account God has no duty to prolong anyone's life and issues, rather than obeys, obligations. It is also insisted that this was an unrepeatable circumstance rather than a standing permission — because the reading's obvious danger is that someone will apply it again.

quote.text: the conquest of Canaan represented God's just judgement upon those peoples
quote.author: William Lane Craig
quote.work: Slaughter of the Canaanites (Question of the Week)

counter.objection: If 'what God commands is just' can absorb the killing of infants, then the word 'just' has stopped meaning anything a worshipper could recognise — and the moral argument of topic 10 collapses with it, because that argument depends on our being able to tell that some things are monstrous. A defence that saves God's goodness by making it unrecognisable has given away what it set out to protect. Randal Rauser, Eleonore Stump and Eric Seibert all press this, and the historical premise is weak besides: the descriptions of Canaanite practice come from the conquering side, and archaeology does not support a picture of exceptional depravity.
counter.sharedPremise: it argues from premises the position holds — that God exists, that Scripture is authoritative, and that we can recognise an atrocity when we see one — to the conclusion that a defence which makes God's goodness unrecognisable has surrendered the thing it set out to protect.
counter.response: Recognising that something would be monstrous for us to do is compatible with its not being monstrous for the one who gives and takes life. The distinction is not invented for this case; it is the ordinary structure of moral permission.

sides.label: A good God would not have commanded it, so the text is wrong about him

arguments.claim: Either these commands were good, or the book that reports them got God wrong
arguments.explanation:
Wes Morriston's version is careful and is addressed to Christians rather than about them. It does not begin from a claim that the Bible is worthless, but from one most Christians already accept: that killing children is wrong, and that we know this as securely as we know anything moral.

The argument runs as a dilemma. God, being good, would command such a thing only for morally sufficient reasons; it is very hard to see what those could be, given that an omnipotent being had every other option; so the more reasonable conclusion is that the text is mistaken about what God commanded. That conclusion is available to a Christian — and unavailable to one who holds [[inerrancy]], which is why the argument bites hardest exactly where the doctrine is strongest.

quote.text: thoughtful Christians who hold the Old Testament in high regard must come to terms with passages in which God is said to command what appear to be moral atrocities
quote.author: Wes Morriston
quote.work: Did God Command Genocide? A Challenge to the Biblical Inerrantist, Philosophia Christi 11

variants.label: The texts are what they are, and the discipline should stop rescuing them
variants.oneLine: The argument is not that a good God would not have commanded it, but that scholarship has spent two centuries inventing reasons why an ancient text still speaks to us, and should stop.
variants.summary:
Avalos's position is aimed at biblical studies rather than at Christians, and it takes the field's own results seriously. Critical scholarship has established that the Bible comes from cultures whose views of the world's origin, nature and purpose are not ones anyone now holds — including most believers. The conclusion he draws is that the various techniques for keeping it relevant are not scholarship but its opposite.

On this account the readings set out on the theist side above are not four attempts at truth but four instances of the same manoeuvre, and the interesting question is why a profession keeps performing it.

quote.text: The Bible is thus largely irrelevant to the needs and concerns of contemporary human beings.
quote.author: Hector Avalos
quote.locator: the thesis of the book, in the author's summary of it

variants.changesTheObjection: The reply above cannot start. It says we are not placed to survey the reasons an omniscient being might have — but this version makes no claim about God's reasons at all, and is not asking whether the command was justified. It is a claim about what a discipline is doing, and an argument about divine epistemic access is simply not addressed to it.

objection.text: The argument uses the field's findings to reach a conclusion the field does not license. That a text comes from a culture unlike ours establishes distance, not irrelevance, and by that standard Homer, Thucydides and Roman law would go too. Reviewers in the same critical tradition — who share the conclusions about authorship, dating and historicity — have argued that 'relevant' is a value judgement smuggled in as a result, and that a professional literature does not stop being worth having because its object is not authoritative.
objection.sharedPremise: it accepts the critical results in full — the dating, the authorship, the historicity, the cultural distance — and argues from those same results that distance is not irrelevance, and that no finding of the field entails the field should end.
objection.response: The comparison fails on the money and the institutions. Nobody funds a thousand chairs of Homeric studies on the premise that Homer is authoritative, and it is that premise, not the texts, that the argument is aimed at.

counter.objection: The dilemma assumes we are placed to survey the reasons an omniscient being might have, and the same move is rejected by most atheists when it appears in the problem of suffering as the 'noseeum' inference. If our inability to see a reason does not settle the case there, it does not settle it here. The argument also proves less than it appears: its conclusion is that a doctrine of inerrancy is false, which most Christians in the world have never held.
counter.response: The comparison fails on the difference between permitting and commanding. Declining to prevent a harm for reasons we cannot see is one thing; instructing someone to inflict it is another, and it is the instruction that is in the text.

arguments.claim: Every one of these readings appeared after the objection, and each appears when the previous one fails
arguments.explanation:
This argument is about the pattern rather than about any single reading. Hyperbole, accommodation, the cruciform thesis and judgement are all set out above, and they are mutually inconsistent — the text either records a real command or it does not.

What they have in common is timing. None was the standard reading before the modern moral objection became forceful, and each becomes prominent as the one before it draws fire. A set of explanations that can absorb any result, and that arrives in the order pressure is applied, is behaving the way a rationalisation behaves rather than the way a discovery does.

quote.text: The proposed readings are inconsistent with one another and none was the dominant reading before the modern moral objection; a family of explanations that arrives in the order the pressure is applied is exhibiting accommodation rather than discovery.
quote.author: Wes Morriston
quote.work: Ethical Criticism of the Bible: The Case of Divinely Mandated Genocide, Sophia 51(1)
quote.locator: our summary of the objection Morriston presses against the standard replies; not his wording

counter.objection: The dates do not support the claim. Origen read these passages non-literally in the third century, and the [[accommodation]] principle is in Calvin — both long before Enlightenment moral criticism. That new readings appear when a question becomes pressing is also how every field works, including this objection, which is itself a modern development of a much older complaint. Timing tells you when people started looking, not whether they found anything.
counter.response: Origen allegorised most of the Old Testament, so his reading of these texts is not evidence of a moral scruple about them in particular. The readings above are recognisably twentieth-century, and their proponents say so.

notes.heading: What the ground says
notes.text:
The archaeology is not in dispute between the readings above, and all of them have to accommodate it. There is no evidence of a mass invasion of Canaan from outside, and no destruction-layer pattern matching the account in Joshua. Jericho's walls appear to have been in ruins for a century or more before any plausible date for the conquest. The current mainstream reconstruction has early Israel emerging largely from within Canaanite society rather than arriving to destroy it.

This cuts in more than one direction. It removes the historical atrocity, which matters. It does not remove the text, and the moral objection is to a book that presents God as commanding this — a book that was read, and acted on, for three thousand years after whatever did or did not happen.

quote.text: about as certain as you can be about these things that the conquest of Canaan as the Bible describes did not happen: no mass invasion from the outside by an Israelite army, and no extermination of Canaanites as God commanded
quote.author: Peter Enns
quote.locator: Enns reporting the consensus among biblical archaeologists

notes.heading: The texts that argue with the texts
notes.text:
The Old Testament is not univocal about this, and reading it as though it were is an error both sides make. Jonah is a story about a prophet furious that God spares a foreign city. Ruth's heroine is a Moabite, from a people Deuteronomy bars from the assembly. Amos has God saying he brought the Philistines from Caphtor as he brought Israel from Egypt, which removes the special claim the conquest rests on.

This does not answer the objection and is not offered as an answer. It bears on a narrower question: whether the conquest texts represent the settled mind of the tradition that carried them. They were preserved alongside their own contradiction, by editors who evidently saw no need to remove either.

whereItStands:
Nothing about the evidence is going to move this, which is why the tag is what it is. The archaeology is settled enough that every reading above has already accommodated it, and the philological question about the conquest formula touches only one of them.

What is contested is a question of judgement: whether a text presenting God as commanding this is best explained as conventional rhetoric misread by moderns, a real and terrible judgement, a misunderstanding recorded honestly, or a distortion God bore. Each explains the same evidence. Each has a cost its holders accept and its critics find intolerable.

One thing has moved. The straightforward judgement reading is markedly less dominant among Christian scholars than it was fifty years ago, and accommodation markedly more so, and that shift happened under moral pressure rather than under new evidence. Both sides point at that fact: one as a tradition correcting itself, one as a tradition retreating.
commonMistake:
Christians most often reach for whichever reading answers the objection in front of them, without noticing they have used three incompatible ones in a single conversation — the commands were hyperbole, and were deserved judgement, and were the Israelites' misunderstanding. Each is a serious position. Held together they are not a position at all, and an interlocutor who notices will reasonably conclude the conclusion was fixed before the readings were chosen. That is what the four panels above are for: pick one and live with what it costs.

Atheists most often quote the passages and stop, as though nothing further were required. Something further is required, because the question is not whether the sentences are shocking — everyone agrees — but whether the reading that makes them shocking is the right one. Refusing to engage the genre argument is refusing the only part of the exchange that could go anywhere.

Both sides also treat the archaeology as settling something. It removes an atrocity from history and leaves the text exactly where it was.
